summary: Provides a framework for Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP), which supports the discovery and exchange of IP telephony gateway routing tables between providers. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: TRIP is a framework for service providers to share information about gateways that can place calls to telephone numbers. Each provider decides which routes to accept and share.

subtitle: A framework for exchanging routes to gateways that connect IP calls to telephone networks.

tldr.problem: A call from an IP network to a telephone number may be handled by many gateways. The best gateway depends on provider agreements, policy, capacity and supported features.
tldr.mechanism: Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP) lets Location Servers exchange gateway route information between administrative domains, applying local policy and optionally combining number ranges.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2871 defines the framework and roles, not the detailed TRIP protocol. It is an Informational memo.

facts.label: Minimum route information
facts.value: Reachable number range and application-layer next hop

today: RFC 2871 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Choosing a Telephone Gateway
sections.content:
An IP caller needs a telephony gateway to reach a phone on a circuit-switched network. Many gateways may be able to complete the call, but provider relationships, policies, capacity and protocol compatibility affect which one can be used.

Because different providers follow different rules, the memo says a single global gateway directory is not suitable. Providers exchange gateway information and build local route databases that reflect their policies.
sections.plainLanguage: Several gateways may reach the same phone number, but a provider cannot necessarily use all of them. It keeps a list shaped by its agreements and rules.

sections.title: What TRIP Covers and How It Differs from BGP
sections.content:
TRIP addresses one mapping task: finding a gateway that can complete a call to a telephone number on a circuit-switched network. It does not find the IP address of a phone-numbered Internet host or the Internet terminal belonging to a telephone subscriber; the memo describes those as directory problems.

TRIP borrows ideas from BGP but runs at the application layer between servers. It exchanges routes to gateways and ranges of phone numbers, not IP prefixes, and it does not aim to connect every administrative domain globally.
sections.plainLanguage: TRIP answers which gateway can reach a telephone number. It does not translate every phone number into an Internet address, and it is not a replacement name for BGP.

sections.title: Domains, Gateways and Location Servers
sections.content:
An Internet Telephony Administrative Domain (ITAD) contains resources managed by one authority and has at least one Location Server (LS). An ITAD may have gateways, end users, both or neither. It need not match an autonomous system.

The LS keeps a Telephony Routing Information Base made from local gateways and remote routes learned through TRIP, applying local policy. A gateway route minimally identifies a reachable telephone-number range and an application-layer next hop. Additional attributes can describe capacity or service, but more detail makes aggregation harder.
sections.plainLanguage: Each provider has at least one Location Server. It combines information about local and remote gateways, then uses provider policy to decide what to keep and share.

sections.title: Exchanging and Aggregating Routes
sections.content:
Location Servers use persistent associations to exchange gateway routes. Administrators establish these peer relationships; TRIP defines the message information but does not dictate the business agreements or routing policy.

An LS may combine several reachable number ranges into one advertised route and identify itself or another signaling server as the next hop. The RFC describes this as a scalability trade-off: more route attributes provide more information but make aggregation more difficult.
sections.plainLanguage: Location Servers exchange lists over configured peer connections. They can combine nearby number ranges into one route, but extra details can make lists harder to combine.

sections.title: Protecting Route Information
sections.content:
Incorrect gateway routes can misdirect calls and spread to other administrative domains. The memo says peer Location Servers need mutual authentication and message integrity.

TRIP messages can reveal an organization's routing capabilities, so the framework also supports encryption. Aggregation changes route objects, which limits end-to-end authentication to the point after the last aggregation.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers need to check who sent a route and whether it changed. They may also encrypt route information to keep it from revealing network details.
